畿.meaning: Around the palace, guards plant a <part>spear</part> at the edge of every <part>rice field</part> and tie it with a <part>twist</part> of red ribbon. Everything inside the ribbons belongs to the city: farms, ponds, even the frogs, who now pay taxes. That's the <kanji>capital area</kanji>.
畿.on: In return the frogs get a big brass <sound>key</sound> to the city gate.
畿.kun: '<sound>Me</sound>, mayor!' croaks the biggest frog. He wears a sash of <sound>ya</sound>rn and rides a <sound>ko</sound>ala to work.

瞳.meaning: A <part>juvenile</part> owl at night school stares into a mirror as the lights go off and watches the black dot in each <part>eye</part> swell up huge. It's the best in the class at just one thing: it has the biggest <kanji>pupil</kanji>.
瞳.on: Its teacher rewards it with a lump of cookie <sound>dough</sound>.
瞳.kun: '<sound>Hee</sound>!' giggles the owl, <sound>to</sound>ssing a crumb of it to <sound>me</sound>.

厘.meaning: A farmer builds his <part>farm</part> on a ledge halfway down a <part>cliff</part>. The field is so small that the cow stands on one leg, and he sows exactly three seeds. Every harvest he gets just a <kanji>tiny bit</kanji>.
厘.on: He trades the whole crop at market for one thin brass <sound>rin</sound>g.

桟.meaning: A family of squirrels drags a soldier's old <part>spear rack</part> to a <part>tree</part> and ties its bars into steps and planks all the way up the trunk. Now they can paint the bark from top to bottom. They've built a <kanji>scaffold</kanji>.
桟.on: At the very top, they share a <sound>sun</sound>dae with a cherry on it.
桟.kun: They lay a plank to the next tree, and a <sound>cu</sound>p of <sound>ke</sound>tchup rolls across to the <sound>hu</sound>t where <sound>she</sound> lives: a plank bridge.

挨.meaning: On a rocking deck, a sailor grips the <part>anchor</part> chain and inches toward the darts board, <part>elbow</part> tucked in, one wobbly step at a time. He can't hit it from the far end, so he walks right up and presses the <part>dart</part> in by hand. Bullseye, if you <kanji>approach</kanji> close enough.
挨.on: The board hangs on a mast covered in <sound>i</sound>vy.
挨.kun: '<sound>He</sound> did it! <sound>Rah</sound>!' cheer the crew, and they push open the hatch to tell the captain.

拶.meaning: At <part>evening</part>, a fishing boat zips home through the harbour's <part>speed zone</part>, its <part>anchor</part> rattling. Right behind it, a black storm cloud closes in, so near that the skipper can smell it. He sniffs once: rain must <kanji>be imminent</kanji>.
拶.on: The skipper peels a <sound>sats</sound>uma to calm his nerves.
拶.kun: '<sound>Se</sound>nd for <sound>Ma</sound>ma!' he shouts as the cloud draws close.

倹.meaning: A man spends his holiday at a <part>campsite</part> in his own back garden to save money. He hangs his one coat on a <part>coat hook</part> nailed to the fence, cooks beans over a candle and uses the same tea bag five times. He calls himself <kanji>frugal</kanji>.
倹.on: He even rents out his dog's <sound>ken</sound>nel as a spare tent.
倹.kun: At night he sneezes in the cold, '<sound>Tsu</sound>!', and warms his hands on an empty <sound>mu</sound>g.

賦.meaning: A <part>warrior</part> who would rather be a poet goes door to door collecting one <part>shellfish</part> from each family for the king. To soften the blow, he recites a little poem with every one he takes. Still, nobody likes the <kanji>levy</kanji>.
賦.on: Back home he counts the haul lying on his rolled-out <sound>fu</sound>ton.

鯨.meaning: The mayor of a sleepy seaside <part>capital</part> orders the biggest <part>fish</part> in the ocean for the city aquarium. It arrives, swallows the tank in one gulp, then blows a fountain over the town hall. Not really a fish at all: a <kanji>whale</kanji>.
鯨.on: Its spout pushes the town's water <sound>ga</sound>uge right up into the red.
鯨.kun: The aquarium <sound>coo</sound>k drives its lunch over in a <sound>jee</sound>p, then has to <sound>ru</sound>n from the splash.
